papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for End-to-End Self-Driving
papers.abstract: End-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving models achieve strong planning performance but remain largely opaque, limiting observability and trust. We apply mechanistic interpretability to E2E driving by training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on the internal activations of a simple, single-camera end-to-end path planning model. Unsupervised clustering of SAE latents reveals interpretable structure aligned with route intent, vehicle speed, and braking behavior, recovering route intent with 98.3% accuracy without supervision. Through paired counterfactual image edits, we further show that specific SAE features are visually grounded and systematically respond to scene changes such as traffic light state and stop sign presence. Steering individual SAE latents produces predictable, monotonic changes in planner outputs including lateral displacement, curvature, and braking. Finally, we demonstrate a practical application of these representations: we build a lightweight adapter trained on SAE latents that reduces trajectory selection error by 3.44%, outperforming an equivalent adapter that omits SAE latents, confirming that the sparse representation captures useful information for interpretability. Code and visualizations are available at this https URL

papers.title: Veloxity: Towards Memory-Safe UAV Embedded Firmware using the Rust Programming Language
papers.abstract: Recent years have witnessed increased momentum towards memory-safe programming languages for safety-critical systems. Memory-safe languages can eliminate entire classes of common software errors that have historically required extensive analysis and expenditure to avoid. Nevertheless, memory-safe language adoption in aerospace remains fragmented and incomplete, particularly for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Recent Rust UAV projects either run only in simulation, are closed source, or have not been integrated with an established autonomy ecosystem and tested against existing C/C++ firmware. To address this gap, we present Veloxity: an open-source embedded UAV autopilot written in the memory-safe Rust programming language. Veloxity lowers the barrier to using memory-safe languages within modern ecosystems by providing a minimal, modular foundation for autonomous UAVs. We compare Veloxity to equivalent autopilots written in C++ in simulation, with hardware testbenches, and via outdoor waypoint-following flight tests, demonstrating functional parity with improved performance. These results indicate that modern memory-safe languages are a viable option for reliable and performant firmware for autonomous aerospace systems.

papers.title: Contact Imitation Interface: Transferring Dexterous Skills by Showing How Contact Unfolds
papers.abstract: Robot-free human demonstrations offer a promising route to scaling dexterous manipulation data. The key challenge is to preserve the demonstrator's natural dexterity while producing contact-grounded observations and actions that transfer to robot hands. We present Contact Imitation Interface (CIMI), a framework with contact-grounded demonstration and learning interfaces. The demonstration interface combines shared contact geometry and fingertip RGB views with contact-alignment-first retargeting and reprojection of wider scene views. The learning interface introduces a hierarchical policy in which a contact-surface planner predicts relative contact-surface trajectories and a controller coordinates wrist and finger commands to improve contact alignment. CIMI combines contact-grounded observations, retargeting, and action representations, improving mean final-stage success by at least 50 percentage points over baseline policies across six hand-task pairs on LEAP and Wuji. Hardware designs and software are publicly available.

papers.title: STAR: Steering Action Representations during Inference
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions, showing strong capabilities across robotic manipulation tasks. However, in our probing experiment, we find that action representations near the action output do not fully preserve task-relevant visual grounding. Motivated by this late-layer grounding gap, we introduce STAR, for STeering Action Representations, a training-free inference method for pre-trained VLAs. STAR applies an exponential moving average over late-layer residual updates, allowing later action representations to inherit object-aware update directions from earlier layers without model updates or architectural changes. It further uses recent proprioceptive states to adapt the mixing strength, using conservative mixing when execution dynamics change rapidly. Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show that STAR improves late-layer object awareness and increases average task success rates by 4.0 percentage points. Our code is available at this https URL .

papers.title: Confidence-Modulated Safety Filtering for End-to-End Policies
papers.abstract: End-to-end policies, from task-specific controllers to robot foundation models, learn complex behavior from raw observations but are not guaranteed to remain safe, so they are often wrapped in a safety filter. The resulting system operates under two domains: the filter's operational design domain (ODD), where its assumptions hold and safety is certified, and the policy's competence domain, where it is reliable. Filters typically fix their conservativeness regardless of the policy's competence, trading performance inside the ODD against margin beyond it. We ask whether the policy's confidence should set that level, and propose a filter-agnostic pipeline that modulates it at runtime: inside the ODD, where every setting is safe, confidence buys performance; beyond it, low confidence adds margin, which helps when it flags where the filter's model fails. Preliminary F1TENTH simulations, where this holds, show the modulated filter combining the strengths of permissive and conservative filters.

papers.title: FlapSim: A Composable MuJoCo Simulation Platform and Reduced-Order Aerodynamic Model Hierarchy for Flapping-Wing Robotics
papers.abstract: Flapping-wing simulation must reconcile high-frequency wingbeat aerodynamics with the slower dynamics relevant to flight control and reinforcement learning. We present FlapSim, a modular open-source MuJoCo simulation platform that combines robot descriptions, wing geometry, and composable aerodynamic models in a deterministic simulation pipeline. Across $48$ held-out scenarios spanning frequency, gimbal, wind, frequency-step, gust, and cross-robot flat-plate regimes, we compare five reduced-order configurations operating at $1\,\text{ms}$ with a $50\,\mu\text{s}$ quasi-steady blade-element reference. The built-in hover cycle-averaged baseline achieves a $67.51\times$ CPU speedup but only $0.6593$ mean wrench fidelity. Combining multirate $21$-substep clock synchronization, three-dimensional linear/quadratic inflow and gust coupling, analytical blade-element geometry scaling, and phase-locked $1f\text{--}6f$ harmonics raises mean fidelity to $0.9646$ at a $65.19\times$ speedup in a five-block model. A streamlined four-block model without explicit step-transient lag states achieves $0.9662$ fidelity at a $67.98\times$ speedup. Controlled ablations show that stroke harmonics are particularly important during frequency transitions, improving held-out frequency-step fidelity by $+0.3176$. Transfer-function analysis explains this effect: fixed-window cycle averaging retains harmonic contributions when the wingbeat frequency changes, so within-cycle reconstruction also improves the filtered wrench. Once phase alignment and harmonic synthesis are included, explicit transient lag states provide no additional benefit in this benchmark. These results characterize the accuracy--computation tradeoff of the aerodynamic hierarchy and identify timing, inflow, geometry, and harmonic representation as central considerations for reduced-order flapping-wing simulation.

papers.title: From Teleoperation to Long-Horizon Dexterity: Evaluating Visuomotor Skills and Offline Proxies for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.abstract: Imitation learning policies are intended to make robotic manipulation robust to variations in object pose, appearance, and environment that challenge pre-programmed motion. However, real-world performance remains difficult to predict, as conventional optimization signals such as validation loss show no consistent relationship with robot success. To identify the design choices that govern real-world performance, 281 imitation-learning policies spanning seven policy families were evaluated in approximately 1,700 real-robot trials of RJ45 connector grasping and insertion using a five-fingered robotic hand. Controlled ablations showed that observation and action representations dominated conventional optimizer and sampling choices. For point-cloud policies, region-of-interest cropping, representation in the robot-base frame, and normalization within the point encoder each improved success by 70-100 percentage points. For the vision-language-action policy, absolute rather than relative action prediction improved insertion success by up to 70 percentage points. Skill decomposition, multi-view perception, and recovery demonstrations were associated with the strongest-performing systems, although their effects were not independently isolated. Of 67 offline metrics evaluated, only five measures of predicted-motion smoothness and directness reliably correlated with insertion success (r = -0.70 to -0.80), and only within a single policy family. These results identify representation choices as key determinants of real-world imitation-learning performance and show that offline metrics can shortlist policies, but cannot replace real-robot evaluation.

papers.title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents
papers.abstract: Across coding, web, and tool-use tasks, language-model agents are now routinely trained with the same recipe: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the interface, then multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) to master it. Code-as-policy (CaP) casts robot manipulation in the same form, as the policy writes code against robot APIs and reads back the results, so the same recipe should apply. Yet existing CaP agents sidestep training: they either prompt closed frontier models or delegate manipulation to pre-trained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and high-level skills, while small open vision-language models (VLMs) fail outright. We present CaPtain, an open post-training pipeline that turns a small open VLM into a capable CaP agent, with no VLA, frontier model, or privileged state at test time. CaPtain trains and deploys the policy inside CaPtain-Harness, which exposes low-level perception, geometry, and guarded-motion primitives across simulation and real hardware. We first align the base model via SFT on synthetic trajectories generated with GPT-6 Astra, then apply multi-turn RL. Multi-turn RL must credit tens of agent requests, whose physical effects often surface turns later, from a single end-of-episode outcome. We therefore introduce a physical critic that reads privileged simulator state, never seen by the policy, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success. Starting from Qwen3.5-4B (0% zero-shot), CaPtain-4B reaches 55.4% held-out LIBERO success after SFT and 73.8% after RL. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 78.5%, surpassing several frontier-model agents, and its RL gains persist across three perturbation suites (+17.6 to +21.2 points). Without target-domain training, it attains 83.3% on SimplerEnv WidowX, exceeds frontier models on CaP-Bench, and runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. We release all code, data, and model weights.

papers.title: WorldBridge: Bridging Video and Action for Task Generalization in World Action Models
papers.abstract: Achieving the broad task generalization of embodied models in physical environments remains a central challenge in robot learning. We study this challenge in World Action Models (WAMs) through two complementary capabilities: video generalization, which predicts the visual evolution of new tasks, and action generalization, which translates these predictions into executable behavior through a video-to-action bridge. By varying video and action supervision for tasks outside an initial training set, we examine their respective contributions to task transfer. On RoboTwin 2.0, using only in-distribution video-action supervision yields a 25.07% success rate on out-of-distribution tasks. Introducing videos of these tasks without their action labels raises success to 55.90%, while adding just one action-labeled demonstration per task further improves it to 70.70%. These findings suggest that broader video coverage enables task transfer by leveraging existing inverse-dynamics capabilities, while even sparse action supervision further strengthens those capabilities. Guided by this perspective, we introduce WorldBridge, a WAM with separate video and action experts connected through structured attention and trained with joint flow matching. WorldBridge incorporates visual memory at two temporal scales and action forcing, alongside a unified data processing pipeline that standardizes and filters heterogeneous robot trajectories and egocentric hand-derived supervision. Across multiple manipulation benchmarks, WorldBridge achieves state-of-the-art performance among the compared methods, including 96.23% on RoboTwin 2.0 full data setting and 80.9% on clean to random setting, 82.8% on RoboCasa GR1 TableTop, and 57.6% on DOMINO Level-1. Our study highlights the complementary roles of video prediction and action grounding in developing robots that generalize across tasks.

papers.title: CausalWAM: Learning the Causes of Actions in World Action Models
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) learn latent variables from observations and use these to both predict the evolution of the scene and to generate actions. The prediction has to be of the whole scene, whereas only a portion of the scene causes actions. WAMs fitted to demonstrations do not, in general, guarantee that they will generate actions solely from the latent causes of the demonstrated actions (the action-relevant latent variables), as the model could just as well learn to imitate in this way whilst entangling the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance variables. We therefore separate out what causes action from what prediction depends on. We prove that under a sparsity constraint the latent variables used to generate actions are an invertible function of the action-relevant latent variables alone and the true structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables. This requires neither sufficient temporal dependence nor any assumptions on how the unobserved regimes evolve and holds even when the action-relevant latent variables are statistically dependent on the rest. We therefore propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which incorporates the constraint into a pretrained WAM by adding a sparse routing path to its action head, with the world modeling objective remaining unchanged. Experiments on both synthetic data and real-world robots validate the theory as well as showcase the improved efficiency in closed-loop success.

papers.title: Sensorium: An Open-Source Multimodal Data Collection and Curation Library for Embodied Surgical AI
papers.abstract: Embodied surgical AI requires reliable multimodal data, yet surgical data collection remains costly, difficult to repeat, and strongly dependent on the hardware setup. We present Sensorium, an open-source Python library for recording, processing, annotating, and curating multimodal surgical data from configurable robot and sensor streams using the Robot Operating System (ROS) and ROS2 middleware. The library combines operator-facing data acquisition, configurable processing, semantic annotation, and episodic dataset generation. We evaluate Sensorium across 1516 recordings of phantom, ex vivo, and in vivo porcine experiments involving multiple surgical tasks and sensing configurations, and report preliminary usability feedback.

papers.title: PGGT-Loc: Primitive-Grounded Geometry Transformer for Feed-Forward Camera Localization
papers.abstract: Camera localization methods are mostly multi-stage pipelines relying on dedicated and complex maps that are costly to construct, store, and maintain over time. Alternatively, well-structured maps that organize scenes with compact yet expressive primitives are often readily available, providing rich structural and semantic cues that humans can interpret. However, their potential for direct camera localization remains largely unexplored due to the significant modality gap between map primitives and visual observations. This motivates a new concept for localization, which estimates camera poses by grounding query observations to map primitives. In this paper, we instantiate the concept in the context of planar primitives with PGGT, the Primitive-Grounded Geometry Transformer network. Given a single query image and a set of planar map primitives, the network is trained to predict multiple localization targets for feed-forward 6-DoF camera localization that generalizes to unseen environments. With this straightforward and scalable architecture, our method pushes the state-of-the-art localization performance on both dense surface maps and minimal layout models. The code and models are available at this https URL

papers.title: DrawSplat: Atlanta World-Guided Implicit Gaussian SLAM for Indoor Reconstruction
papers.abstract: RGB-D SLAM requires accurate online tracking, high-quality rendering, and geometrically consistent reconstruction. Existing Gaussian SLAM methods mainly optimize Gaussian primitives with photometric, depth, or local frame-to-model constraints, which are often insufficient in indoor scenes with weak textures, large planar structures, noisy depth, and long trajectories. The resulting maps may suffer from pose drift, surface thickness artifacts, noisy normals, and blurred structural boundaries. We propose DrawSplat, an Atlanta World-guided implicit Gaussian SLAM framework for indoor reconstruction. DrawSplat follows a drawing-like process: explicit point-line geometry first sketches the structural layout, and implicit neural Gaussians then fill in high-fidelity appearance and continuous geometric details. It estimates camera poses, sparse geometry, and gravity direction through point-line joint tracking, infers structural planes from tracked lines using the shared-gravity component of the Atlanta World prior, and converts them into differentiable regularization terms on Gaussian centers and normals. To improve compactness and efficiency, DrawSplat further combines an anchor-based implicit neural Gaussian representation with adaptive structural sampling, which allocates Gaussian capacity to structurally informative regions. Experiments on multiple datasets show that DrawSplat achieves robust tracking, high-fidelity rendering, and strong geometric reconstruction among Gaussian-based SLAM systems, while maintaining a practical balance among quality, efficiency, and model size.

papers.title: FOCUS: First-Order Control Using Optimal Transport Supervision for Imitation from Observations
papers.abstract: Imitation learning from observations must recover behavior from state-only demonstrations without known temporal correspondence. Differentiable simulators provide pathwise policy gradients, but differentiating through long, contact-rich trajectories can make optimization unstable. We introduce FOCUS, which combines local optimal-transport alignment with short-horizon differentiable actor-critic learning. FOCUS matches agent rollout windows to multiple sampled expert segments using a soft best-of-$K$ objective that emphasizes locally compatible matches. The resulting transport-based costs provide differentiable imitation rewards, while a learned critic bootstraps value beyond the rollout horizon. FOCUS requires neither temporally aligned trajectories nor expert-aligned initialization or teacher forcing. Across contact-rich locomotion tasks in DFlex, including a musculoskeletal humanoid controlled by 152 muscle activations, FOCUS improves sample efficiency and training stability over adversarial imitation-from-observation methods and prior differentiable imitation baselines.

papers.title: SACQ: Structure-Aware Codebook Quantization for Ultra-Low-Bit Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable capable robot behavior, but their large memory footprint limits deployment on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Weight quantization is a natural remedy, yet post-training quantization (PTQ) recipes inherited from large language models degrade when applied to VLAs at ultra-low precision. Existing low-bit PTQ methods often fail to explicitly account for the structure of downstream operations and allocate precision without considering its effect on the policy actions. We introduce SACQ, an ultra- low-bit weight-only vector-codebook quantization framework for VLAs. SACQ combines (1) structure-aware codebook fitting with role-specific quadratic metrics that reflect input statistics and downstream sensitivity; (2) action-aware mixed-bit allocation based on the increase in final-action error as individual layers are compressed; and (3) two-stage post-quantization refinement that reassigns codeword indices with second-order error compensation and calibrates codebooks and row-group scales against the decoded action. Using GR00T N1.7, SACQ achieves 93.85% average success across four LIBERO suites at 1.5 bits per language/action weight while reducing model memory by 4.83x. With INT8 activation quantization and low-precision attention, it retains 93.55% success while running 1.51x faster than BF16. On SimplER, SACQ further achieves 63.76% and 52.27% success under Visual Matching and Variant Aggregation at 2 bits per language/action weight, compared to 58.90% and 53.45% for BF16, respectively.

papers.title: MotorSense: A Video-EMG Dataset of Motoric Representations for Action Understanding
papers.abstract: Computer vision models learn hand action only from its visual consequences, without access to the underlying embodied motor signals. We address this absence with MotorSense, the first large-scale paired egocentric video and surface electromyography (EMG) dataset. MotorSense pairs bimanual EMG bands with egocentric video and yields synchronized video, bimanual EMG and IMU, and audio across 100 hours of unscripted manipulation. EMG offers a powerful scalable alternative to manual annotation: it captures finger movement, hand configuration, and the forces exerted between hand and environment as a dense signal free of occlusion and labeler bias, whereas manual annotation is costly, subjective, and unreliable under occlusion. We use MotorSense to learn sensorimotor alignment, producing an organization of action that is shared across the visual and motoric spaces, through cross-modal pre-training between video and EMG. The resultant vision models are then transferred to downstream tasks that benefit from sensorimotor alignment: in this case, action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction, and 3D contact reconstruction. We further demonstrate a generative application in which EMG motor signals are used to condition a video diffusion model, yielding videos of fine-grained hand manipulation. Across four action-centric computer vision tasks and eight popular video datasets, we demonstrate that sensorimotor alignment provides a stronger foundation for visual representation learning than conventional self-supervised learning methods over video, outperforming every baseline across all tasks and datasets evaluated.

papers.title: Consensus Within, Competition Between: Decentralized LLM Teams for Perimeter Defense
papers.abstract: The use of large language models (LLMs) to coordinate multi-agent teams raises a fundamental architectural question: whether task allocation should be centralized in a single LLM controller or distributed across autonomous LLM agents, particularly when communication is unreliable. In a deliberately simplified perimeter-defense simulation against LLM-controlled intruders, we compared a central commander, an auction-based consensus team and independent agents under five network conditions. Breach rates were 15% for the consensus team, 32% for the commander and 29% for independent agents, and of the different network conditions, only limited radio range changed a team's breach rate, raising the commander's. In consensus team, giving a low-cost LLM more authority over the bid computation raised breaches by 38 percentage points. With birds and civilian drones in airspace, we added a photograph for each to the input text state. Only the near-frontier model treated them apart from intruders. Intruders disguised as existing taxidermy bird drones were mistook as birds by both low-cost and near-frontier LLMs, going unpursued in 59-61% of near-frontier decisions (1-16% before). However, a one-sentence forewarning in the prompt lowered it to 0-25%. We find that LLM team with a dedicated external conflict resolution protocol results in fewest breaches. Code: this https URL .

papers.title: CuPIQP: A Batched and Differentiable QP Solver on GPUs for Robot Learning and Control
papers.abstract: Quadratic programs (QPs) are fundamental building blocks of many robotic tasks such as inverse kinematics, whole-body control, and model predictive control. Extending these methods to large-scale robot learning and control requires solving many QPs concurrently and, for end-to-end learning, differentiating through their solutions. Efficient batched optimization is therefore essential to bringing established model-based methods into GPU-based robotics pipelines. We present \textsc{cuPIQP}, a batched and differentiable QP solver on GPUs based on a proximal interior-point method, with unified support for dense, sparse, and multistage problems. The solver exploits parallelism across independent QPs and their internal structure while preserving per-problem numerical updates and termination decisions. Benchmarks with up to 16384 QPs per batch demonstrate solve-time speedups of up to $18.8\times$ over \textsc{Moreau} and $4.26\times$ over eight-core \textsc{PIQP}. In an end-to-end learning task, \textsc{cuPIQP} accelerates training by $4.6\times$ over \textsc{QPAX} and $7.8\times$ over \textsc{Moreau}. papers.title: Robot Navigation and Canine Welfare: A Pilot Study Surfacing Challenges for Cross-Species Legibility and Proxy Validity in Animal-Machine Interaction
papers.abstract: Autonomous delivery robots increasingly share residential spaces with companion animals, yet navigation behavior is rarely designed with animal welfare in mind. This paper presents a pilot study evaluating a curve-out maneuver, a laterally arcing pass-by trajectory triggered at the dog's alert distance, proposed as a candidate welfare-informed navigation intervention grounded in canine social communication research and legible motion theory. Following a research through design approach, we developed and evaluated a first design iteration of the artifact in a naturalistic home environment with a companion dog. Contrary to our hypothesis, the curve-out produced a more acute stress response than the straight-line baseline. We argue that discontinuous execution limitation, the robot stopping and reorienting multiple times to approximate the arc, undermined legibility, which in itself became a stressor. The pilot surfaces the legibility of robot behavior to non-humans' eyes and proxy stimulus validity as structural challenges for AMI and repositions the design problem for future work.

papers.title: AquaProbe: Efficient Adaptation of Frozen Vision Models for Underwater Images
papers.abstract: Reliable visual perception is essential for safe autonomous underwater exploration. Yet vision models pretrained on terrestrial images become less reliable underwater, where turbidity, backscatter, and wavelength-dependent attenuation alter scene appearance. Existing adaptation methods either spread adapters equally across the encoder depth or select layers using the divergence between two fixed domains. In this paper, we introduce AquaProbe for measuring how the location of the domain gap changes with water type and imaging range. AquaProbe separates newly introduced divergence from that accumulated through a frozen vision encoder using paired clean and physically rendered images and allocates a fixed LoRA budget according to the measured profile. The segmentation mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU) for the proportional LoRA rank allocation, based on the measured profile, is 70.1; this is a better result than uniform LoRA rank allocation by 1.9 mIoU points while having the same parameter budget of 0.59 million adapter parameters. The three-way router, conditioned on estimated condition clusters, achieves 70.6 mIoU on the standard SUIM split and 63.4 AUDRC under held-out degradation.

papers.title: How a group that cannot communicate knows itself by its enemy
papers.abstract: Teams that cannot communicate seem stuck with what each member sees. We show that their opponent can tell them the rest. Silent hunters, jammed robots and traders who never meet all face an adversary that reacts to the group as a whole; every member can read that reaction, a tell, and learn what no member knows alone. One tell can do the work of a message from every member. The adversary would rather hide, but hiding interferes with its own task, and a team that commits in advance to how it will respond decides how much hiding is worth. A committed team never loses when its opponent cares more about its own goals, and does as well as a fully informed team exactly when the opponent's stake outweighs any gain from lying. Below that point the team learns more by trusting less: in a solved Gaussian model it obtains the truth by promising not to use all of it and keeps the cost the opponent would have paid to conceal; an exact test decides when this holds in finite games. How a team spreads its trust matters too. A lone uninformed member with a full-support prior needs a private coin, but with additive squared-error losses two interchangeable members who respond differently replace it, and a small discount on trust insures against misjudging the enemy. Information, on this view, is not only gathered or aggregated; it is produced by how a team commits to respond.

executive_summary: Several works advance scalable optimal control and optimization for robot motion: Sequential Contact Insertion (SCI) parameterizes multi-robot trajectories via contact events and analytically reconstructs minimum-energy, collision-free paths for double-integrator robots, planning for up to one million robots in minutes with median speedups of several orders of magnitude over a fixed-grid sequential convex programming baseline while matching its solution accuracy; a companion analysis for two double-integrator robots with squared-acceleration cost proves all optimal collision-free trajectories fall into eight contact families and provides a geometric characterization and numerical solver; and cuPIQP introduces a batched, differentiable GPU quadratic-program solver based on a proximal interior-point method that yields up to 18.8× and 4.26× solve-time speedups over Moreau and an 8-core PIQP implementation, respectively, and accelerates a differentiable-robot-learning pipeline by 4.6×–7.8× over existing QP solvers.

New safety and certification frameworks target heterogeneous and formally guaranteed control: the Capability-Aware Backup-Recoverability Filter (CA-BRF) constructs capability-dependent backup-recoverable sets and filters navigation commands so multi-robot teams remain recursively feasible and safe even when nominal safety optimization fails, validated in simulations with up to 30 heterogeneous robots and hardware tests on five kinematic classes; the Capability-Conditioned Heterogeneous Graph Control Barrier Function (CC-HGCBF) uses Radial Capability Fields to encode robot-specific reachable velocities, enabling decentralized, zero-shot safe navigation and coordination for mixed teams of seen and unseen platforms in simulation and physical trials; AC-SMPC embeds an explicit-constraint MPC layer in an actor–critic framework, with the actor tuning MPC objectives and an elastic QP relaxation handling local infeasibilities, improving multi-robot navigation efficiency in dynamic, narrow environments while maintaining safety compared to existing MPC-based baselines; and Proof-Carrying Evolution (PCE) evolves controllers together with formal certificates, showing that enforcing certification during search consistently produces certified docking controllers and that language-model-guided synthesis can outperform classical baselines on linear problems, while CMA-ES and hand-tuned designs remain competitive on SO(3).

Multiple systems leverage large models and harness design to improve embodied control: REA (Routed Embodied Agent) coordinates deliberative, routed, and reactive policies under budgeted escalation and judge-gating, achieving 95.9% success on 3,000 LIBERO-Pro episodes (vs. 94.7% for the best single policy) with 25% fewer control steps and 17% less control time, and 84–86% success on RoboTwin 2.0 versus 80% for the strongest VLA baseline while also transferring to BEHAVIOR-1K and a real humanoid; RoboArchitect uses a coding model to iteratively edit the agent harness around a frozen policy, boosting average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks by discovering improved control logic and memory without changing policy weights; LEXP wraps a multimodal reasoner (ChatGPT-6-Astra) with an experience module that extracts and reuses lessons from prior executions, raising success over 12 real-world manipulation tasks to 63.9% versus 52.8% with memory alone and 5.6% with vanilla Astra, with ablations showing both planning and experience retention are critical; and Proof-Carrying Evolution demonstrates that language models can participate in certified controller design by proposing candidate laws with accompanying proofs checked during search.

New benchmarks and datasets expose limitations of current policies and provide richer supervision: MolmoSpaces-CommonSense defines a manipulation benchmark grounded in developmental cognitive science to test occlusion, containment, support, grasp semantics, and hidden-object reasoning, finding that zero-shot generalist policies suffer >50% success drops with added distractors, select wrong objects ~30% of the time in clutter, succeed only ~50% on affordance-sensitive grasps even with targeted language prompts, and that VLM-based rollout scoring is unreliable in these scenes; MotorSense releases 100 hours of egocentric video paired with bimanual EMG, IMU, and audio, showing that cross-modal video–EMG pretraining yields sensorimotor-aligned visual representations that outperform video-only self-supervision across four action-centric tasks and eight datasets and enable EMG-conditioned diffusion to generate fine-grained manipulation videos; and a large-scale real-robot study of 281 imitation-learning policies for RJ45 grasping/insertion shows that observation/action representations (e.g., point-cloud cropping, robot-frame coordinates, encoder normalization, and absolute vs. relative action choices) dominate optimizer/sampling effects, with some choices improving success by ~70–100 percentage points, while only five smoothness/directness-related offline metrics correlate (r = -0.70 to -0.80) with real insertion success and only within a single policy family.

Several methods propose new policy and world-model formulations for generalist and dexterous control: CWAM augments world action models with a sparse routing path so that, under a sparsity constraint, action-generating latents provably become an invertible function of action-relevant variables alone, with synthetic and real-robot experiments indicating more efficient closed-loop task success; Hourglass factorizes planning into a body-agnostic world model and robot-specific differentiable ego-dynamics, allowing a single parameter-conditioned policy to match per-robot specialists and trail a parameter-conditioned MPPI teacher by only 1.4–2.8 percentage points across seven simulated robots, while transferring zero-shot from synthetic training to a new real skid-steer platform after ~3 minutes of dynamics identification; DiffWBC uses a one-step diffusion controller over humanoid trajectories to achieve the lowest local tracking error among six trackers (20.1 mm on BONES), support 50 Hz control on a Unitree G1, enable strong zero-shot test-time steering (e.g., 0.84 vs. 0.10 clean passes under a low ceiling), and identify likely physical failures with 91% precision in the top 2% high-dispersion rollouts, half of which are fixed by targeted fine-tuning; DMAT models bimanual joint-space action chunks directly on an action manifold with stochastic interpolants and STR refinement, outperforming Improved 3D Diffusion Policy and DiTFlow3D by 129.1% and 95.7% relative success, respectively, while generating actions 1.34–2.06× faster and remaining robust under repeated 50 N disturbances; and HandMimicX trains dexterous object-centric reinforcement learning policies from egocentric human RGB-D videos by optimizing object motion with hand–object interaction constraints, with simulations and real-robot trials indicating efficient skill learning and generalization to new spatial configurations.

New hardware and fielded systems demonstrate sim-to-real transfer and autonomous inspection: an open-source knee exoskeleton and biological torque controller trained purely in musculoskeletal simulation, without device-specific data, reduce peak biological knee extension moment by 21.5% and vastus medialis activation by 26.7% during squats in seven participants compared to unassisted squatting (p<0.05), showing that simulation-trained torque estimation can transfer directly to hardware; and SAFARI integrates semantic detections as probabilistic channels into a unified map to guide frontier-based exploration and risk-aware planning, yielding 98.7% average coverage of accessible area and 97.6% autonomy across 11 quadruped missions in three complex field sites while detecting hazardous objects as small as 15 cm, with ablations underscoring the importance of object-size awareness and safety-aware path planning.

institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes sequential contact insertion (SCI), an optimization algorithm that parameterizes multi-robot trajectories via contact events at minimum separation, solving a coupled algebraic system in contact variables and reconstructing trajectories analytically between contacts for double-integrator robots with minimum-energy objectives and collision-avoidance constraints. institution_matches.title: A complete analytical characterization of optimal collision-free motion for two robots
institution_matches.overview: The paper analytically characterizes optimal collision-free trajectories for two robots under double-integrator dynamics with a squared-acceleration objective, assuming both robots start and end at rest. The authors argue that insights from this analytical structure can be used to improve the performance of existing numerical trajectory optimizers for multi-agent motion planning.

institution_matches.title: MolmoSpaces-CommonSense: Evaluating Commonsense in Robotic Manipulation Policies
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces MolmoSpaces-CommonSense, a robotic manipulation benchmark and taxonomy grounded in developmental cognitive science that targets commonsense reasoning skills such as occlusion, containment, support, semantically appropriate grasp points, spatial affordances, and inference about hidden objects in cluttered settings. Zero-shot generalist manipulation policies evaluated on MolmoSpaces-CommonSense exhibit substantial commonsense failures: success rates in cluttered scenes decrease by over 50% as distractors increase, policies act on incorrect objects about 30% of the time in clutter, and affordance-sensitive grasping achieves correct object-part selection only about 50% of the time even with specific language prompts. institution_matches.title: Proof-Carrying Evolution: Black-Box Search, White-Box Flight
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes proof-carrying evolution (PCE), a controller-design framework in which a search procedure, potentially guided by a language model, generates candidate controllers together with formal certificates of their properties; certificates are checked during search and only certified candidates can be returned, with the deployed artifact consisting of the control law plus its certificate. institution_matches.title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces RoboArchitect, a system in which a coding model observes rollouts from a frozen robot policy, diagnoses failure modes, and iteratively edits the surrounding agent harness—including control logic, tool use, and memory—so that the harness, rather than the policy weights, is adapted to a new robot or benchmark. The evolved harnesses automatically discover intuitive control strategies (e.g., lifting a jammed arm or approaching horizontally when blocked from above) and implement persistent memory that carries experience such as effective grasp depths into later decisions, suggesting that significant performance headroom lies in automating harness design rather than further finetuning base policies.

institution_matches.title: MotorSense: A Video-EMG Dataset of Motoric Representations for Action Understanding
institution_matches.institution: Carnegie Mellon University; Massachusetts Institute of Technology
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces MotorSense, a 100-hour egocentric dataset that pairs synchronized video with bimanual surface EMG, IMU, and audio during unscripted hand-object manipulation, positioning EMG as a dense, occlusion-free, and scalable alternative to manual annotation for capturing fine-grained hand configuration, finger movement, and interaction forces. topic_matches.title: From Teleoperation to Long-Horizon Dexterity: Evaluating Visuomotor Skills and Offline Proxies for Dexterous Manipulation
topic_matches.overview: The paper reports an empirical evaluation of 281 imitation-learning policies from seven policy families on about 1,700 real-robot trials of RJ45 connector grasping and insertion with a five-fingered robotic hand, finding that observation and action representations have a larger impact on real-world performance than optimizer or sampling choices. Out of 67 offline metrics examined, only five measures related to predicted-motion smoothness and directness correlate reliably with real-robot insertion success (correlation r = -0.70 to -0.80), and only within a single policy family, indicating that such offline proxies can shortlist policies but do not replace real-robot evaluation.

topic_matches.title: A Capability-Aware Backup-Recoverability Filter for Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Navigation
topic_matches.institution: Texas A&M University; University of Illinois Chicago
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes the Capability-Aware Backup-Recoverability Filter (CA-BRF), which constructs a capability-dependent backup-recoverable set in a shared Cartesian operational space by certifying pairwise-safe backup maneuvers that bring heterogeneous robots to rest while respecting each robot’s kinematic and actuation constraints. topic_matches.title: Capability-Conditioned Graph Control Barrier Functions for Zero-Shot Safe Navigation of Heterogeneous Mobile Robot Teams
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces the Capability-Conditioned Heterogeneous Graph Control Barrier Function (CC-HGCBF), defined in a shared second-order reference-point operational space, to provide a common safety representation for heterogeneous robots while preserving their individual dynamics and control constraints. topic_matches.title: Learning from Physical Experience:Context-Space Adaptation for Robotic Manipulation
topic_matches.institution: The Chinese University of Hong Kong; University of Electronic Science and Technology of China; xdof.ai
topic_matches.overview: The paper empirically shows that a general-purpose multimodal reasoner, ChatGPT-6-Astra, can function as a context-responsive manipulation policy in real-world experiments, exhibiting effective fine manipulation and spatial reasoning when given a suitable action interface. topic_matches.institution: MeiTuan; NVIDIA; The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen; TsingTec; Tsinghua University
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents HandMimicX, an object-centric reinforcement learning framework that learns dexterous manipulation skills from egocentric human RGB-D videos by optimizing an RL objective over object motion, thereby decoupling the learned skill from specific human hand trajectories. topic_matches.title: DiffWBC: Unlocking Steerable General Humanoid Motion Tracking via One-Step Diffusion Whole-Body Control
topic_matches.institution: Shenzhen University of Advanced Technology; Southeast University; Southern University of Science and Technology; The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces DiffWBC, a one-step diffusion-based whole-body controller that models distributions over future humanoid trajectories, enabling a single generative controller to perform general motion tracking, zero-shot test-time steering, and simulation-free failure discovery. topic_matches.title: SAFARI: Semantic- And Frontier-driven Autonomous Risk Inspection
topic_matches.institution: Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (ETH Zürich)
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes SAFARI, a semantic- and frontier-driven autonomous risk inspection framework that integrates object detections as a native probabilistic channel in a unified map, allowing geometric and semantic evidence to jointly guide exploration and motion planning in hazardous environments. topic_matches.title: AC-SMPC: Differentiable Actor--Critic MPC with State Constraints for Safe and Fast Robot Navigation
topic_matches.institution: Chinese Academy of Sciences Shanghai Institute of Microsystem and Information Technology; Soochow University
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents AC-SMPC, an actor–critic model predictive control framework that embeds a differentiable MPC layer with explicit state constraints for safe navigation, representing robots and obstacles with vertices and the workspace with half-spaces, and convexifying hyperplane-based collision-avoidance constraints within the MPC optimization. In AC-SMPC, the actor learns to adjust MPC objective parameters via closed-loop feedback to shape local motion behavior, while the critic evaluates long-term task performance, and the MPC layer is relaxed into an elastic quadratic program using bounded penalized slack variables to handle cases where local constraint approximations are infeasible. Simulation and hardware experiments on multi-robot dynamic collision avoidance in narrow environments indicate that AC-SMPC improves navigation efficiency and adaptively adjusts the learned policy while maintaining safety, compared to existing navigation and MPC-based approaches.

topic_matches.title: Direct Action-Manifold Modeling for Efficient and Robust Bimanual Manipulation
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes the Direct Manifold Action Transformer (DMAT), which models observation-conditioned bimanual joint-space action chunks directly on an action manifold using stochastic interpolants, enabling single-step action generation without iterative denoising or numerical integration as in diffusion or flow-matching visuomotor policies. DMAT leverages local 3D scene geometry to anchor predictions and introduces State-Consistent Spectral-Time Refinement (STR) to reconcile predicted action chunks with proprioception and attenuate high-frequency residuals, improving temporal consistency and robustness.
